channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: A magnitude-7.7 earthquake off Indonesia's Flores island forced thousands to evacuate, record rain and a typhoon flooded Japan's Chiba region, and Colombia's recovery from its own quake has paralysed coffee exports — adding fresh strain to supply chains.
item.description:
A powerful magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck off Flores island in Indonesia's East Nusa Tenggara province on 15 August, killing dozens and forcing more than 3,300 people to evacuate as roads were cut; the state utility restored most power and the national oil company assured fuel supplies were secure. In Japan, record rainfall and Typhoon Chan-hom flooded Chiba prefecture, disrupting transport, briefly isolating Narita airport and leaving over 22,000 households without power. In Latin America, the aftermath of Colombia's earlier magnitude-7.4 quake continues to bite: landslides and blocked roads have paralysed coffee exports — a blow to a top global supplier — and President de la Espriella asked Washington to suspend tariffs given the damage, with China's Zoomlion sending relief machinery. Separately, insurers reported that global natural-disaster losses in the first half were lower than recent peaks (Aon about USD 47 billion), even as the frequency of events rises.

Industry Impact

Clustered natural disasters across manufacturing-heavy Asia and commodity-exporting Latin America are a recurring reminder that supply chains face physical, not just political, disruption. Japan's floods threaten electronics and auto-parts output in an already tight chip environment; Indonesia's quake hits a growing manufacturing and resource economy; Colombia's coffee halt shows how a single event can choke a globally traded commodity. For materials suppliers, the lesson is resilience — mapping exposure to disaster-prone nodes, holding buffer inventory for critical inputs, and monitoring second-round effects on commodity prices and logistics. The dip in insured losses offers little comfort given the rising frequency of severe events.

Chinatimes | Business Recorder | Antara News | Channel News Asia | MarketScreener | ANSA | Der Standard

item.title: France's maize crop could halve and EU output fall to its smallest in decades, Swiss dairy farmers face a feed shortage, and Ukraine's grain exports have nearly stopped after Black Sea port attacks — prompting a global food-price warning.
item.description:
Europe's fifth heatwave of the summer is turning a weather story into a food-supply one. Relentless heat and drought could halve France's maize harvest and cut EU cereal production to its lowest in decades, despite steadier crops in Poland and Romania. Switzerland's dairy sector faces a critical shortage of animal feed, Hungary's prime minister warned drought damage could exceed the devastating 2022 season, and wildfires have hit France's Landes, Germany's Hesse and the English Midlands. The UK authorised GBP 65 million in extra aid for drought-hit farmers after the driest July on record. Compounding the supply shock, Ukraine — a major grain exporter — has nearly halted shipments after renewed attacks on its Black Sea ports and civilian vessels, and the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization warned of a possible surge in world food prices. Analysts estimate the drought could cost the EU economy around EUR 180 billion this year, erasing much of its projected growth.

Industry Impact

Beyond the direct hit to agriculture, the drought is a supply-chain and input-cost story with second-round effects for industry. Low rivers disrupt barge transport of chemicals and raw materials (see other insight in this alert), reduced hydropower and reactor cooling strain energy supply, and rising crop and feed prices feed into costs for bio-based and food-adjacent materials, packaging and coatings. Higher global food prices also squeeze consumer budgets in emerging markets, dampening demand. Companies should treat extreme-heat disruption to European logistics and energy as a recurring seasonal risk to plan around, not a one-off.

Arab News | Neue Zürcher Zeitung | The Guardian | Süddeutsche Zeitung | MarketScreener | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Anadolu Agency

item.title: Investment in China's "embodied intelligence" robots topped CNY 93.5 billion in the first half, five times a year earlier, its core AI industry passed CNY 1.2 trillion, and LG and NVIDIA agreed to co-develop a next-generation humanoid robot.
item.description:
China's push into physical AI is accelerating. Financing for "embodied intelligence" — AI built into robots that act in the real world — exceeded CNY 93.5 billion in the first half of 2026, a fivefold jump year-on-year, while the country's core AI industry surpassed CNY 1.2 trillion in scale across more than 6,200 firms, with related sectors growing over 30%. The momentum is regional and corporate: the Tianjin robotics cluster lifted output 15.2%, and innovative drugs, AI and robots are being promoted as China's new industrial "business card". The technology race is not China's alone — South Korea's LG signed a deal with US chipmaker NVIDIA to build a next-generation bipedal humanoid robot on NVIDIA's robotics platforms, targeting a first-quarter unveiling. The wave follows the blockbuster Shanghai listing of humanoid maker Unitree, whose retail tranche was thousands of times oversubscribed.

Industry Impact

The capital surge into robotics and physical AI is building a large new demand base for advanced materials — lightweight structural composites, adhesives and bonding for actuators and joints, protective and functional coatings, sensors and battery systems. China's scale and state backing give its robot makers a cost and deployment advantage that will shape global competition, while the LG–NVIDIA tie-up shows the humanoid race is now a US–Korea–China contest. For materials suppliers, industrial automation and humanoid robotics are a structural growth channel; positioning early with robot and component makers — especially in China's fast-moving ecosystem — will matter for capturing it.

China Economic Net | Xhby.net | Associated Press | MarketScreener | South China Morning Post

item.title: In his 15 August address Prime Minister Modi called India the fastest-growing major economy of the past 12 years, said three semiconductor plants are already producing with five to eight more coming, and set a 200-gigawatt nuclear target.
item.description:
Marking India's 80th Independence Day, Modi framed the country's rise "from Fragile Five to fastest-growing" and laid out a self-reliance roadmap built on what he called seven streams (Sapta Dhara): manufacturing, agriculture, technology, energy and more. The headline industrial claim was on semiconductors — production has begun at three plants, with another five to eight expected over seven to eight years — alongside pledges on mining, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, space and robotics. On energy security he set a 200-gigawatt nuclear target with new reactors. Domestic policy is reinforcing the message: India's recent cut to the goods-and-services tax (GST) is emerging as a crucial buffer for carmakers facing higher commodity costs, helping firms such as Mahindra, Tata Motors and Hyundai protect margins. India also targets chemical exports of up to USD 81 billion by 2030 (see other insight in this alert).

Industry Impact

India is positioning itself as the structural alternative to China in electronics, chemicals and advanced manufacturing, and the semiconductor build-out in particular creates fresh demand for specialty chemicals, coatings and packaging materials used in chip fabrication. For suppliers, the combination of a fast-growing domestic market, tax relief supporting autos, and explicit industrial targets makes India one of the most attractive medium-term growth markets — though execution on power, skills and logistics will determine how quickly the ambitions translate into orders. The GST cut is a near-term positive for the auto value chain and the materials feeding it.

The Statesman | The Times of India | LiveMint | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Business Standard | The Economic Times

item.title: Taiwan raised its full-year growth forecast to 11.05%, the highest in 39 years, with exports seen up more than 40% on artificial-intelligence chip demand, and lawmakers finally passed a long-delayed budget that funds a major drone-industry programme.
item.description:
Taiwan's statistics agency, the DGBAS, revised its 2026 GDP growth forecast up to 11.05% from 9.64% — the fastest pace since 1987 — after the economy grew 14.15% in the first half, powered by exports projected to rise about 41% on surging demand for AI-related semiconductors. The upgrade cements Taiwan as one of the biggest winners of the global AI investment wave. Separately, and after a record political deadlock lasting well over 200 days, Taiwan's legislature passed the island's 2026 central government budget of about USD 93 billion, which was cut by TWD 48 billion during the standoff but retained funding for defence and a TWD 63.4 billion, six-year programme to build up the domestic unmanned-vehicle (drone) industry.

Industry Impact

Taiwan's boom is concentrated in the semiconductor and AI-hardware chain that sits upstream of much of global electronics manufacturing, reinforcing the island's centrality to supply chains — and the concentration risk that comes with it. Strong chip exports pull demand for the specialty chemicals, advanced packaging materials, adhesives and coatings used in semiconductor fabrication and assembly. The new drone-industry funding adds a second materials-intensive growth avenue. For suppliers, Taiwan is a high-growth but geopolitically exposed market; the AI-driven surge is an opportunity, while cross-strait tension remains the standing tail risk to monitor.

Commercial Times | MarketScreener | Lianhe Zaobao | Chinatimes | Al Jazeera | Cnyes

item.title: Trump set tariffs of up to 100% on imported drones from early September, with a 15% rate for close allies, while NATO jets shot down drones over the Baltics and European defence firms moved to mass-produce their own combat drones.
item.description:
President Trump signed a proclamation imposing tariffs ranging from 10% to 100% on imported unmanned aircraft and their components, effective around 3 September, citing national security and heavy reliance on Chinese supply. The top 100% rate applies to large drones and those with thermal-imaging cameras; close allies — the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland — face 15%, and the UK 10%. Taiwan, which secured the lower rate without stacked duties, welcomed the move. The tariff lands as drones become a live security issue in Europe: NATO fighter jets, including Italian and Spanish aircraft, shot down drones that crossed into Latvian and Romanian airspace amid Russian electromagnetic interference, and Finland restricted parts of the Baltic. In response, European industry is scaling up: Rheinmetall is preparing industrial-scale production of unmanned systems, and France's Delair and KNDS have already delivered 460 units of a new "Damoclès" kamikaze drone built in a year.

Industry Impact

Drones are becoming both a trade-policy and an industrial-strategy priority, and the build-out pulls in materials the ACS and advanced-materials sectors supply — lightweight composites, adhesives, coatings, sensors and batteries. The US tariff will reshape sourcing, favouring allied and domestic producers and raising costs for buyers dependent on Chinese hardware. Europe's rush to field its own combat drones signals durable defence demand and new supply chains for specialty materials. Companies positioned in composites, bonding and protective coatings for aerospace and defence should see this as a structural growth channel rather than a one-off procurement spike.

The Hindu Business Line | Commercial Times | Global Times | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Chinatimes | Dawn | Il Sole 24 Ore | Channel News Asia | MarketScreener | Wallstreet:online | TF1 Info

item.title: Fallout from a White House report accusing 40-plus countries of helping China route goods around US tariffs is spreading fast: Singapore has charged three people for faking origins, China rejects the "scam" label, and India was among those flagged.
item.description:
The White House Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy last week labelled over 40 trading partners — including Canada, India, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan — as high-risk conduits in a Chinese "shadow transshipment network", the practice of shipping goods through a third country to disguise their origin and dodge higher US import duties. Trade adviser Peter Navarro put the lost US tariff revenue at USD 19–26 billion a year, and the administration said it will use AI tools to police the trade. The report is already producing action and friction: Singapore Customs charged three individuals and a company with falsifying the country of origin of goods, and Singapore's trade ministry vowed firm enforcement while insisting legitimate supply-chain shifts are not evasion. China's foreign ministry rejected the "transshipment scam" accusation, arguing that normal diversification of production should not be criminalised.

Industry Impact

This escalates tariff enforcement from rates to origins, and it reaches deep into supply chains that legitimately span several countries. Manufacturers that assemble or finish goods in South-East Asia, India or Mexico now face heightened scrutiny of where value is genuinely added, real prosecution risk for mis-declaration, and pressure to document origin rigorously. For the chemicals and materials chain, which routinely moves intermediates across borders before final production, the practical burden is tighter origin tracing and compliance — and the strategic risk that "China plus one" sourcing hubs get caught in the enforcement net. Expect more countries to tighten their own customs rules to stay off Washington's list.

BBC News | Cnyes | The Times of India | Lianhe Zaobao | Global Times | BNN Bloomberg | Channel News Asia | The Straits Times | China Daily | The Economic Times

item.title: Japan's economy grew just 0.3% in the second quarter, well short of forecasts, yet markets now price a likely September rate rise after coordinated yen-buying, and short-term government-bond yields have jumped to multi-decade highs.
item.description:
Japan's gross domestic product rose only 0.3% in the April–June quarter (about 1.1% annualised), below the 2.0% analysts expected and down from an upwardly revised prior quarter, as consumer spending and investment weakened under the drag of the Iran war and higher energy costs. Despite the soft data, the Bank of Japan is moving the other way. Coordinated yen-buying intervention alongside the US and South Korea — aimed at halting the currency's slide — has firmed expectations that the central bank must raise rates to make the support stick, and markets now put the odds of a September hike near 76%. Two-year government bond yields have climbed to their highest in decades. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, meanwhile, finalised a cut to the consumption tax on food and drink to ease the cost of living. The contrast with the US is sharp: benign inflation and flat producer prices there have pushed traders to rule out a near-term Federal Reserve move.

Industry Impact

A BoJ hike into a weakening economy would be a notable turn after years of ultra-loose policy and would lift the yen, raising the cost of Japanese exports but cutting import bills for Japanese manufacturers. For global suppliers, diverging central-bank paths — Japan tightening, the US on hold — mean continued currency volatility that complicates pricing and hedging across regions. Rising Japanese bond yields also pull capital and can ripple into global funding costs. Companies selling into or sourcing from Japan should factor a firmer yen and tighter domestic demand into second-half plans.

Channel News Asia | Jakarta Post | Commercial Times | Handelsblatt | The Standard | The Economic Times | Business Recorder | Chinatimes | MarketScreener | Axios

item.title: China's car sales fell about 20% in July, a tenth straight monthly decline, even as commercial-vehicle exports rose 36% and Iran-war-driven heavy electric-truck exports doubled — with cargo-ship capacity now too tight to move them all.
item.description:
China's domestic passenger-car sales dropped roughly 20% year-on-year in July, extending a run of monthly falls that erased about 2.3 million vehicles of demand in the first half, even as electric and hybrid models took record shares of what buyers remained. The contrast with exports is stark. Commercial-vehicle exports rose 36.1% in the first seven months to 785,000 units, and heavy electric-truck exports more than doubled to 16,823 vehicles in the four months after the war began, as high oil prices made battery trucks attractive in South and Southeast Asia. Demand is now straining logistics: global roll-on/roll-off ("ro-ro") car-carrier capacity — the specialised ships that move finished vehicles — cannot keep pace with Chinese exports approaching ten million units, and sea-freight rates have doubled from pre-pandemic levels. A former BMW-China executive even floated "reverse joint ventures" to let Chinese carmakers into Western markets on controlled terms.

Industry Impact

The split economy inside China's auto sector matters for suppliers on both sides. A weak home market pressures Chinese producers to export ever harder, intensifying price competition in Europe and emerging markets and squeezing the Western carmakers that are core customers for coatings, adhesives and sealants. At the same time the export surge — especially in electric trucks and commercial vehicles — creates demand for battery, lightweighting and bonding materials wherever those vehicles are assembled or serviced. The shipping bottleneck is a reminder that logistics, not just production, is now a binding constraint on China's export drive, and a lever competitors and policymakers can watch.

The Standard | The Straits Times | China Economic Net | Lianhe Zaobao | MarketScreener | BNN Bloomberg | Chinatimes | Yahoo Germany

item.title: Germany's manufacturing sector cut 144,100 jobs in the first half of 2026, its car industry's workforce fell to the lowest since 2005, domestic output kept shrinking, and German firms' investment in the US dropped by two-thirds.
item.description:
Federal Statistical Office data show German manufacturing employment fell 2.7% to 5.29 million in the first half of 2026, a loss of 144,100 jobs, with the automotive industry hit hardest — its workforce down 5.8% to 691,500, the fewest since 2005 and a fall of 42,300 in a year. German car production has slid to 4.1 million vehicles from 4.7 million in 2019. The retrenchment is not only domestic: a German Economic Institute study found German companies invested about EUR 4.3 billion in the US in the first half, down 65% year-on-year, as tariffs and uncertainty deter cross-border projects. Against this backdrop the auto lobby VDA is reportedly reconsidering its previously soft line on tougher EU trade policy toward China, as Chinese competition erodes German brands at home and in export markets.

Industry Impact

Germany is the largest single market for many industrial suppliers, and a shrinking manufacturing and automotive base directly lowers demand for the adhesives, coatings, sealants and engineered materials that go into vehicles, machinery and construction. The job losses are structural, not cyclical — driven by high energy costs, Chinese competition and weak investment — so suppliers should not expect a quick rebound and should weight growth plans toward Asia, North America and India. The VDA's possible shift toward supporting trade defence against China signals that even Germany's export-dependent carmakers now see Chinese competition as an existential threat, which could reshape the European policy debate on tariffs and local-content rules.

Die Zeit | Handelsblatt | Bloomberg | Yahoo Germany | La Nacion

item.title: Germany's economy minister backed EU plans to weaken the emissions-trading scheme and Washington pressed Brussels to loosen its sustainability and carbon-border rules, while the Rhine fell to a record low and new packaging rules burdened smaller firms.
item.description:
Pressure to lighten Europe's regulatory load on industry is building on several fronts. German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche welcomed EU Commission proposals to soften the Emissions Trading Scheme — the system that makes companies pay for carbon they emit — warning it must not "overburden" the economy. Washington, in parallel, urged the EU to ease its Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (which holds large firms responsible for environmental and labour harm in their supply chains) and its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (a tax on the carbon content of imports); European panel makers separately asked Brussels to exclude urea from that carbon-border tax. The chemical industry association VCI warned Germany is squandering its innovation potential amid deindustrialisation. Physical stress compounds the policy strain: the Rhine has fallen to its lowest level since records began, limiting barge loads to plants such as BASF, and EU packaging rules in force since 12 August are adding compliance costs for small firms. India, meanwhile, set a target to lift chemical exports to USD 81 billion by 2030.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) chain this is the clearest sign yet that Europe's regulatory direction is turning from tightening to relief — a potential easing of carbon and due-diligence costs that have weighed on European producers versus Asian and Middle-Eastern rivals. But the benefit is uncertain and slow, while the immediate costs are real: record-low river levels raise inbound feedstock and outbound logistics costs across the German chemical cluster, and the new packaging regime lands first on smaller suppliers. Watch two things — whether the ETS and sustainability-rule softening actually reaches statute, and how long the Rhine stays unnavigable. India's export ambition is a reminder that the competitive map keeps shifting toward lower-cost, policy-backed producers.

Handelsblatt | Yahoo Germany | MarketScreener | Cnyes | Channel News Asia | Politico Europe | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Neue Zürcher Zeitung | Il Sole 24 Ore | The Hindu Business Line | China Economic Net | PCI Magazine

item.title: A 50% US tariff on about USD 20 billion of Canadian goods takes effect on 19 August with no deal in hand, though both sides call the talks "constructive" and Washington may cut car and metals duties under a limited "phase one" agreement.
item.description:
Canada's negotiators, led by trade minister Dominic LeBlanc, warn there may be no way to avert the new tariffs due Wednesday, which would hit goods that do not qualify under the North American trade pact. Yet the picture is not one-way: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called the latest round "constructive", and reports say Washington may reduce its "Section 232" tariffs — duties imposed on national-security grounds — on Canadian cars, steel, aluminium, copper and lumber, and drop a further tariff threat, in exchange for a narrow "phase one" deal. The catch is that the US insists it will not accept any Canadian retaliation. Separately, Detroit's carmakers are lobbying against a US plan to rewrite the North American trade agreement (USMCA), warning it could add more than USD 2 billion a year to each company's costs and erode their competitiveness against foreign rivals.

Industry Impact

For manufacturers with cross-border supply chains, Wednesday is a genuine inflection point: either a punitive 50% wall goes up on non-qualifying goods, or a partial rollback eases the metals and auto duties that most affect industrial inputs. Companies should ready both scenarios — confirming which products meet North-American origin rules to escape the tariff, and stress-testing costs if steel, aluminium and copper duties stay. The episode underlines that even close US allies now face abrupt, deadline-driven tariff swings, making origin compliance and dual-sourcing a standing requirement rather than a contingency for the chemicals and coatings chain that supplies autos and construction.

La Presse | CBC | BNN Bloomberg | POLITICO | The Globe and Mail

item.title: The US said it can blockade Iran's ports indefinitely and will unveil new isolation measures next week, as the 60-day ceasefire expires and Vice President Vance called low oil prices — not Iran's nuclear programme — the war's first goal.
item.description:
The conflict that began with Israeli and US strikes on 28 February has settled into an economic siege centred on the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel through which much of the world's seaborne oil passes. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said American forces can sustain a naval blockade of Iran's ports "indefinitely", and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent promised "unprecedented" measures next week to stop goods entering or leaving the country. The 60-day US–Iran ceasefire lapses this weekend, and tankers belonging to the UAE's Adnoc were attacked overnight in the Gulf. To cushion the supply loss, Washington is releasing 172 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve — the emergency government oil stockpile — cutting it to about 243 million barrels. Iraq lifted exports to a wartime-high two million barrels a day. Prices rose on the week but Brent still sits roughly USD 40 below its April peak near USD 126, as China has redirected discounted Iranian and Russian crude and eased the squeeze.

Industry Impact

Vance's admission that the priority is cheap fuel for American consumers signals Washington will manage the war to avoid an oil-price spike rather than force a rapid escalation — a relief for energy-intensive manufacturers, but no route to a settlement. For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) sector the key variables remain feedstock and freight: naphtha and other oil-linked inputs stay volatile, diesel is flagged as a bigger risk than crude (Goldman Sachs), and Gulf shipping and insurance costs stay elevated. Pipeline demand is one bright spot — India's MAN Industries is expanding on Gulf orders. Plan for a prolonged, capped-price war, not a near-term normalisation.
